MandiGuard — The Complete Student Study Guide

Phantom Spatial Arbitrage in Indian Mandis: Stage I (MandiGuard) + Stage II (MandiGuard-CRC)
Explained from first principles — so that any Class 10–12 student can follow every step
Why this topicFirst principlesData collection Data validationMethod (step by step)Fair testing ResultsStage II autopsy & fixRelated papers What we did differentlyLimitationsSynopsis slides Viva Q&A
The whole thesis in 3 sentences A price on a mobile screen can show that a mandi 200 km away pays ₹600 more per quintal, but after the truck reaches, the market may be closed, the exact variety may not be bought, diesel and fees cost money, and tomatoes rot in the heat — so most of that “extra money” is a phantom. We measured this with real government price data (69,526 real dispatch opportunities, 6 states, 4 crops) and built MandiGuard, a checklist-style decision helper that checks the cheap facts first, keeps a safety cushion, and says “stay home” when the trip is risky. Then we honestly examined why it did not beat a strong simple rule on average, fixed three causes (MandiGuard-CRC), and tested the fix on data it had never seen.
How to use this guide Read Chapters 1–3 to understand the idea. Chapters 4–9 are the research journey in order (data → method → testing → results). Chapters 10–12 cover papers, novelty and limitations. Chapters 13–15 prepare you for the synopsis presentation and viva. Yellow boxes = intuition, blue = key facts, purple = maths, green = what to say in the viva, red = traps to avoid.

Chapter 1 — The Story: Why This Topic?

1.1 Meet the farmer

Imagine a small tomato farmer in Madhya Pradesh. This morning he can sell his harvest at the local mandi (wholesale market) for ₹1,400 per quintal (1 quintal = 100 kg). On his phone, a government price portal shows that a mandi 200 km away paid ₹2,000 per quintal. That looks like ₹600 extra per quintal.

How big is this for him? The Government of India’s National Statistical Office survey (NSS Report No. 587) says onion and potato households typically harvest about 29–39 quintals per season — roughly one 30-quintal mini-truck — and the average agricultural household earns only about ₹3,798 per month from crops, with 50.2% of households in debt (average ₹74,121).

Why the stakes are high ₹600 × 30 quintals = ₹18,000 of apparent extra income from one truck — close to five months of average crop income. A wrong decision is equally large in the other direction: diesel is spent, produce rots, and the farmer may have to sell cheaply or drive back.

1.2 The trap: the screen price is not the price you will actually get

Between seeing a price on the screen and getting cash at the far mandi, four real-world frictions eat the gap:

  1. Wrong variety or grade: buyers bid separately for, say, Red vs Desi onions, or Grade A vs Grade B apples. If nobody is buying your exact variety that day, you sell at a discount.
  2. Closed gates and old (stale) quotes: mandis have weekly holidays and sometimes simply do not report prices. The ₹2,000 you saw may be 4 days old, or the market may be shut on the day your truck arrives.
  3. Real roads are longer than straight lines: in Himachal Pradesh, 91.59% of motorable roads (39,465 of 43,091 km) are single-lane hill roads (HP Economic Survey 2025–26). Diesel and time cost more than a map line suggests.
  4. Heat, rain and fees: tomatoes rot faster in a 40°C afternoon; heavy rain damages produce; states charge different market fees (0.5% to 1.5%).

We call the part of the screen gap that disappears “Phantom Spatial Arbitrage”: spatial = between places, arbitrage = buying/selling to profit from a price difference, phantom = it looks real but vanishes.

1.3 How big is the phantom? (our first measurement, Exp 1)

We replayed what would happen if farmers simply chased the best screen price (we call this policy B1) on real data from June 2025 to April 2026:

What we measured (63,040 naive truck dispatches)Value
Average screen gap the farmer saw₹1,330.49 / qtl
Average money actually gained after everything₹386.02 / qtl (71% smaller)
Lost to diesel + fees₹160.81 / qtl
Lost to heat/rain spoilage (modelled)₹68.76 / qtl
Lost to closed gates, missing variety and arrival-day price drops₹714.90 / qtl
Trucks that hit a closed gate or missing-variety delay58.94%
Trucks that lost money compared with selling at home40.46%
The surprising part The biggest loss is not diesel or rot. It is “execution risk”: arriving and finding the market closed or not buying your variety. A smarter price forecast alone cannot fix that, because the problem is not just “what will the price be?” but “will I even be able to sell there?”
Figure 1 (thesis numbering). Where the apparent profit disappears for naive screen chasing (Exp 1).

1.4 Why we chose this topic (the reasons you should say in the synopsis)

ReasonExplanation
Real social valueSmallholders earn little; one bad truck trip can wipe out months of income. Helping them avoid bad trips matters.
A clear, measurable gapEconomics papers show price information alone does not raise farmer income when transport and selling are unreliable (Mitra et al., 2018). Computer-science papers forecast prices but rank markets using straight-line distance and ignore closed markets. Nobody had measured how much of the screen gap is phantom across many states and then built a decision rule around it.
Public, checkable dataAGMARKNET prices, OpenStreetMap roads, ERA5/NASA weather and government survey numbers are all public, so anyone can reproduce the work.
Right size for M.TechThe method uses simple, explainable tools (rules + one tree model + a safety cushion) rather than a large black box, so it can be built, tested and defended in one thesis.
Honest science is possibleBecause outcomes are recorded in history, we can test decisions on months the model never saw, and pre-register what we expect before looking.
Say this in the viva (30 seconds) “Price portals made information free, but information is not money. Across 63,040 naive dispatches, a ₹1,330 screen gap turned into ₹386 of real gain, and 40% of trucks lost money — mostly because markets were closed or not buying the exact variety. So I studied the decision — go or stay — not just the price, and built a transparent checker that verifies the cheap facts first, keeps a safety cushion and is allowed to say ‘stay home’.”

Chapter 2 — First Principles: The 12 Ideas You Need

Everything in this thesis is built from twelve simple ideas. Learn these and the rest is just careful bookkeeping.

Idea 1 — Mandi, quintal and the three prices

A mandi is a regulated wholesale market (APMC). Each day the portal records, for each crop and variety, a Min price, a Max price and a Modal price (the most common price). Prices are in ₹ per quintal (100 kg).

Idea 2 — The spread

Spread (what the screen promises) Screen spread = Destination price on screen − Local price at home Example: ₹2,000 − ₹1,400 = ₹600 per quintal.

Idea 3 — Net gain (what you actually earn compared with staying home)

Net gain of a trip (per quintal) Net gain = (Price you really get) × (1 − fraction spoiled) − freight and market fee − waiting charges (if the market is late or closed) − local price you gave up If Net gain is negative, the trip was a loss trip. Staying home (“SELL_LOCAL”) always has Net gain = ₹0.

In the thesis, freight = ₹35 loading + ₹0.45 per km (×1.45 on Himachal hill roads), plus the state market fee (0.5%, 1.0% or 1.5%) on cross-district trips. Waiting costs ₹25 per quintal per day.

Idea 4 — Spoilage grows with heat (the Q10 rule)

Biology rule of thumb: many decay processes roughly double for every +10°C (called Q10 = 2). The government NABCONS survey (2022) gives market-stage losses at a reference condition: Tomato 3.25%, Onion 1.96%, Apple 1.64%, Potato 0.86%.

Spoilage in one line spoiled fraction ≈ base loss × (hours on road / 24) × 2^((temperature − 20) / 10) At 40°C, 2^((40−20)/10) = 2^2 = 4, so decay runs 4 times faster than at 20°C. (The full formula also adds humidity and heavy-rain effects and is capped at 55%.)

Idea 5 — Why the screen can lie: stale, closed, wrong variety

  • Stale: the quote is several days old. Prices may have moved.
  • Closed: the market does not open (or does not report) on the day your truck arrives.
  • Wrong variety: the market is open but nobody is buying your exact variety/grade.

In live checks on 17 November 2026 (Exp 8), 11 of 22 benchmark corridors had no reported price at all for the previous 7 days.

Idea 6 — Average is not enough: loss rate and the worst 10%

Two plans can have the same average but very different risk. So we use four simple metrics:

MetricSimple meaning
Mean Net Gain (₹/qtl)Average extra money per quintal over all opportunities (a “stay home” day counts as ₹0).
Loss-Trip Rate (LTR)Of the trucks that were actually sent, what % lost money.
Worst-10% Loss (CVaR10%)Take the worst 10% of outcomes and average them. It tells you how bad the bad days are.
Live API calls per queryHow many external look-ups (roads, weather, model) we needed — a measure of cost and effort.
Illustration: why worst-10% matters Plan X over 10 trips: +500, +500, +500, +500, +500, +500, +500, +500, +500, −1,500 → average +300, worst-10% = −1,500.
Plan Y over 10 trips: +300 every time → average +300, worst-10% = +300.
Same average, but a poor farmer would prefer Plan Y. This is why we never judge a plan only by its average.

Idea 7 — Every prediction has errors, so keep a safety cushion

A machine-learning model predicts the arrival price, but it is sometimes too optimistic. Instead of trusting the raw prediction, we look at how wrong the model was on recent, already-finished trips, and subtract a cushion large enough to cover most of those errors.

Illustration: the 80% cushion Suppose on the last 10 finished trips the model over-predicted by 1%, 2%, 2%, 3%, 4%, 5%, 6%, 8%, 11%, 15%. The value that 80% of errors stay below is about 8%. So we subtract 8% from the next prediction. If the model’s errors behave like the past, about 4 out of 5 future trips should come in at or above this cautious estimate.

This idea is called conformal prediction (Angelopoulos & Bates, 2023). In MandiGuard the cushion is recomputed from a rolling window of the last 400 matured trips, using only trips whose arrival date has already passed. We checked it on new data: the cushion covered 78.85% of validation outcomes and 79.07% of holdout outcomes — very close to the 80% target.

Idea 8 — Saying “No” is a valid decision (the reject option)

In 1970, C. K. Chow proved that when a wrong decision costs much more than not deciding, the best system should sometimes abstain. For a farmer, a bad trip loses diesel, produce and time, while staying home costs nothing extra. So MandiGuard has an explicit output: REFUSE_PHANTOM_SPREAD (sell locally).

Idea 9 — Ask cheap questions first (the cascade)

Analogy: a doctor A doctor first asks simple questions and checks temperature (cheap), and orders an MRI (expensive) only if needed. MandiGuard does the same: first check “is the market alive for my variety?” (cheap), and only then fetch roads, weather and the model.

Idea 10 — Fair testing: practice paper, mock test, board exam

We split time into three parts, like exam preparation:

2024 = Practice
train the price model
Jan–May 2025 = Mock test
choose settings (₹50 margin)
WALL
Jun 2025–Apr 2026 = Board exam
final test, never used for tuning

Leakage means accidentally using information from the future (like seeing the board exam answers while practising). We built a “firewall” so the model can only use information available on the decision morning.

Idea 11 — Is a difference real or luck? (bootstrap, p-value, Holm)

  • Bootstrap: re-draw the data many times (5,000 times) with replacement and see how much the result wobbles. We re-draw whole origin mandis (174) and whole 2-week blocks (23), because days in the same market or same fortnight are related — treating them as independent would make us over-confident.
  • p-value: roughly, how often a difference this large could appear just by chance if there were no real effect. Small (e.g., below 0.05) = probably real.
  • Holm–Bonferroni: when you test four hypotheses, the chance of one lucky “win” increases, so Holm makes the threshold stricter.

Idea 12 — Pre-registration: write your predictions before seeing results

Before looking at the final test months, we wrote down four hypotheses (H1–H4) and saved them in Git (commit e421d15). This prevents HARKing (“Hypothesising After the Results are Known”) — changing the story after seeing the data. Anything we discovered later is clearly labelled Stage II, post-diagnostic.

Chapter 4 — Data Collection: Where Every Number Came From

Golden rule of this project: no invented price data. Prices, roads and weather come from public sources; cost parameters come from government publications. Anything we had to assume (like truck hire rates) is clearly labelled as modelled.

4.1 The six data sources

SourceWhat it givesSize / coverage
AGMARKNET (Govt of India price portal, via public archive mirror)Daily Min/Max/Modal price per market, crop, variety42,722,187 raw records (2017–2026) → 883,406 rows for our 178-mandi panel
HP Apple graded data (AGMARKNET 2.0 export)Apple prices separated by grade (A, B, C, …)4,427 records, 42 markets; 1,537 test lots
OpenStreetMap + OSRM (road router)Real road distance and driving time between markets8,147 directed corridors (15–500 km)
ERA5 (European reanalysis) and NASA POWERActual temperature, rain, humidity on the roadERA5: 141,955 rows, 145 grid cells (2024–26); NASA: 291,384 rows, 114 cells (2017–23); 0% missing
Open-Meteo forecasts (NWP)What the farmer could know on the morning (forecast, not actual)102 of 145 cells archived; rest filled by a causal Ridge model (MAE 1.047°C)
Government reportsSpoilage rates (NABCONS 2022), state fees (PIB), hill roads (GoHP 2025–26), truck size and income (NSS 587)Fixed parameters, all cited

4.2 Step-by-step: from 14 million rows to a clean 178-mandi panel

Stream14,443,770 records (2024–Apr 2026)
➜
Filter6 states × 4 crops = 681,258 rows
➜
CleanRemove 284 bad prices + 7,003 duplicates
➜
Clean result673,971 records, 699 markets
Eligibility≥ 20 trading days in 2024 and ≥ 80 total (469 markets)
➜
Select using 2024 onlyTop 30 per state by 2024 activity
➜
Fixed panel178 mandis, 260,043 daily records
Why choose markets using only 2024? If we chose markets because they traded a lot in 2025–26 (the test period), we would be quietly using the future — markets that later shut down would be excluded, making results look better. This mistake is called survivorship bias. Choosing with 2024 data only keeps the test honest.

We also harmonised names: generic clerk labels (e.g., “Other”, “FAQ”) became “Standard”; spelling variants were unified (Deshi → Desi); but real commercial varieties (Red, Hybrid, Royal Delicious, …) were kept separate, because variety mismatch is one of the traps we study.

4.3 Placing markets on the map and measuring roads

Market names220 (state, district, market) tuples
➜
Geocode with district checkmust lie ≤ 110 km from district HQ
➜
Coordinates150 exact, 70 district-centre fall-backs
➜
OSRM roads8,147 corridors, 15–500 km
➜
Arrival lag1 day: 3,810 | 2 days: 3,942 | 3 days: 395

Why the district check? Many Indian villages share names across states. Without the check, a market could be placed hundreds of km away. The arrival lag (1, 2 or 3 days) comes from driving time × 1.35 for trucks (plus hill adjustment in HP) plus 4 hours for loading and auction timing.

4.4 Weather: what you knew vs what actually happened

A subtle but important point: on the dispatch morning, the farmer only has a forecast. The truck, however, experiences the actual weather. So we use forecasts to make decisions and actual weather (ERA5/NASA) to score what really happened. Mixing them would be leakage.

Chapter 5 — Data Validation: How We Proved the Data Is Trustworthy

An examiner will ask: “Your bulk prices came from an archive mirror. How do you know they match the government?” This chapter is your answer. Validation happened in five layers.

Layer 1Clean: bad prices, duplicates, names
➜
Layer 2Official parity checks (Exp 14)
➜
Layer 3Location & weather sanity
➜
Layer 4No-future-leakage firewall
➜
Layer 522 automated tests + independent reviewers

5.1 Layer 2 — Comparing our copy with official government data (Exp 14)

CheckWhat was comparedMatched keysMinMaxModal
Tier 1: data.gov.in official XML (18 Oct 2023)6,434 all-India rows → 532 in our states/crops → 181 in our panel172100%100%99.42%
Tier 2: AGMARKNET 2.0 official export (149 trading days)4,427 HP Apple rows → 2,082 inside the mirror’s date window2,042100%100%100%
How to explain it “We took the same market, date, variety and grade from the official government source and from our copy, and compared the rupee values. On 172 keys from a single official day, Min and Max matched exactly and Modal matched 171 of 172. On 2,042 keys spread over 149 days, all three prices matched exactly.” Be honest that this is a strong sample check, not a full re-download of all years.

5.2 Layer 3 — Location and weather sanity

  • Every market coordinate must be within 110 km of its district headquarters (catches same-name villages).
  • Weather grids: 0.0% missing values for ERA5 (2024–26) and NASA POWER (2017–23).
  • Forecast filler (Ridge model) was trained only on 2024 and tested on Jan–May 2025: average temperature error 1.047°C.
  • An extra check on the 42,766 episodes from the 4 states with 100% real archived forecasts confirmed the filler did not distort results.

5.3 Layer 4 — The “no peeking” firewall

  • The price model is trained on 2024 only and then frozen.
  • The safety cushion only learns from trips whose arrival date has already passed on the decision morning.
  • Validation (Jan–May 2025) is only used to choose settings; we also require arrival dates ≤ 31 May 2025 so no validation outcome leaks into June.
  • The code contains an automatic check (assert_no_future_leakage_dates) that stops the program if training dates overlap later periods.

5.4 Layer 5 — Software tests and independent review

22 out of 22 automated tests pass. They check: file checksums (SHA-256), split dates, no-leakage rules, fee and spoilage parameters, bootstrap and Holm arithmetic, and that every result file and figure exists and is consistent. Two independent review agents audited the code, data, results, paper and viva material over three rounds until both returned PASS.

Do not over-claim Tests prove the code is correct and reproducible. They do not prove real-world truck costs or rot rates — those are modelled from government averages and still need field receipts.

Chapter 6 — Building Fair Test Questions: Episodes and Time Splits

6.1 What is an “episode”?

An episode = one farmer, at one origin market, with one crop/variety, on one morning, deciding whether to send a truck, and if yes, to which of the shortlisted destination markets. Each episode is like one exam question. Because history recorded what prices actually were on the arrival days, we can score every decision afterwards.

Morning tFarmer at origin, local price known
➜
Step 0Up to 5 destinations, 15–500 km, screen gap > ₹100
➜
DecisionSend to market j, or stay home
➜
Arrival t+τLook up real price on arrival days
➜
ScoreNet gain, loss?, trap?

6.2 How a real outcome is scored (the three arrival situations)

Situation on arrivalWhat we assume happensLabel
Market open and buying your exact variety on arrival daySell at that day’s real modal priceClean sale
Not buying your variety today, but does within 1–2 daysWait (₹25/qtl/day) and extra rot, then sellDelay trap
Variety never trades in 3 daysSell another variety at Min price −10%, or if the crop is absent, pay 1.5× return freight + rotClosed trap

The last row uses modelled penalties (we cannot observe what a real farmer would have done). That is why Exp 15 tests what happens if these penalties are much smaller or even zero (Chapter 9).

  • The ₹50 safety margin was chosen from {50, 100, 150, 200, 250} using validation data only (validation mean ₹351.36/qtl).
  • During the holdout, the cushion keeps updating, but only from trips that have already arrived — exactly what a real app could do.

Chapter 7 — Stage I Method: MandiGuard Step by Step

MandiGuard is not a chatbot or a self-learning robot. It is a deterministic checklist (same input → same output) plus one frozen tree model and a safety cushion. There is no large language model and no reinforcement learning inside it.

7.1 The decision flowchart (for each shortlisted market)

Step 0 — Free shortlist (0 calls)Up to 5 markets within 15–500 km whose 7-day screen price beats local by > ₹100/qtl
NO ➜
No candidate → SELL LOCAL
↓ YES (pass)
T1 — Is the market alive for my exact variety? (1 call)Quote ≤ 3 days old AND reported on ≥ 50% of last 14 days AND open on ≥ 35% of past same-weekdays
NO ➜
Reject this market (stale / closed / wrong variety)
↓ YES (pass)
T2 — Do roads + fees still leave profit? (+1 call)Real OSRM km/hours, freight ₹35 + ₹0.45/km (×1.45 in HP), state fee
NO ➜
Reject (spread eaten by freight)
↓ YES (pass)
T3 — Will heat/rain rot eat the gain? (+1 call)Morning forecast → Q10 spoilage + rain penalty; gain must stay > 0
NO ➜
Reject (spoilage risk)
↓ YES (pass)
T4 — Cautious profit after the 80% cushion (+1 call)Frozen 2024 tree model predicts arrival return; subtract recent 80th-percentile error
NO ➜
Reject (not safe enough)
↓ YES (pass)
Pick the surviving market with the highest cautious profit. If it is > ₹50/qtl → DISPATCH
else ➜
REFUSE_PHANTOM_SPREAD (sell locally, ₹0 change)
Why this order? T1 is the cheapest check and removes the biggest danger (closed / wrong-variety markets). Removing T1 in testing made traps jump to 67.16% and cut average gain by ₹134.05/qtl. So it makes sense to ask it first and avoid paying for road, weather and model look-ups on markets that are already dead.

7.2 The tree model in simple words

The model is a HistGradientBoostingRegressor — many small decision trees added together, each correcting the previous ones’ mistakes. It predicts the arrival return = (arrival price − reference price) / reference price, using 17 causal features such as recent price changes, volatility, how often the market reports, and calendar effects. “Causal” here means each feature only uses information available on or before the decision morning. It was trained on 2024 and then frozen.

7.3 Worked example 1 — one Tomato trip through the maths (from the thesis)

Madhya Pradesh, 40°C May afternoon, 200 km (6 hours), local ₹1,400, screen ₹2,000 1. Screen price ₹2,000.00 2. Heat spoilage: 3.25% × (6/24) × 4 = 3.25% − ₹65.00 → ₹1,935.00 3. Freight ₹35 + 0.45×200 = ₹125; MP fee 1.5%×1,400 = ₹21 − ₹146.00 → ₹1,789.00 4. 80% cushion: 8% × ₹1,935 − ₹154.80 → ₹1,634.20 5. Minus home price − ₹1,400.00 Cautious net gain = +₹234.20 per quintal (+₹7,026 on 30 qtl) Since +₹234.20 > ₹50 safety margin → DISPATCH. If T1 had found the variety not traded for 5 days, or T3 had found 40 mm rain, the answer would be REFUSE and the farmer keeps ₹0 change instead of risking a loss.

MarketWhat happensCalls used
AT1 fails: quote is 5 days old1

On the real holdout, MandiGuard averaged 8.75 calls vs 15.74 for “check everything” (B4) — 44.4% fewer — with identical profit.

Chapter 8 — Fair Testing: Baselines, Hypotheses and Statistics

8.1 Who did we compare against? (baselines)

A result only means something when compared with sensible alternatives. We used seven comparators:

BaselineWhat it doesWhy include it
B0 Sell localNever sends a truckZero-risk reference (₹0)
B1 Naive screen chasingHighest screen price minus straight-line freight > ₹100What many farmers would do
B2 Fresh + road ruleNeeds a same-day exact-variety quote, real road freight and fees > ₹100A strong simple rule — hard to beat
B3 Point-MLUses ML average prediction + road freight, no T1/T3/cushionLike typical price-forecasting apps
B4 Check everything upfrontCalls all 4 tools on every candidateTests if the ordered cascade saves effort
B5 Multi-agent bucketsRoles talk in coarse LOW/MED/HIGH bucketsTests if exact rupee values matter
B6 Rule-of-thumb routerFixed thresholds and a flat 12% weather cutTests a rigid heuristic

8.2 The four pre-registered hypotheses (written before seeing the test data)

IDHypothesis in plain words
H1MandiGuard earns more on average than naive screen chasing (B1).
H2MandiGuard earns more on average than the fresh + road rule (B2).
H3MandiGuard causes fewer loss episodes than point-ML (B3).
H4MandiGuard needs at least 25% fewer external calls than checking everything (B4).

8.3 How we decided if a difference is real

Pair the policiesSame 69,526 episodes for all
➜
Two-way cluster bootstrap174 mandis × 23 two-week blocks, 5,000 redraws
➜
Exact p-valuePhipson–Smyth (never zero)
➜
Holm correction4 tests, family error 5%
Why “paired” and “clustered”? Paired: every policy faces exactly the same farmers on the same mornings, so differences come from the decisions, not from luck in which days were picked. Clustered: days in the same market and the same fortnight move together (a festival or a strike affects all of them). Re-drawing whole markets and whole fortnights gives honest, wider confidence intervals.

9.3 Robustness: do the conclusions survive tough questions?

Tough questionExperiment and answer
Which check matters most?Exp 4 ablation: without T1, mean drops by ₹134.05 and traps rise to 67.16%; without T4, loss trips rise from 9.97% to 16.89%. T2 (+₹0.44) and T3 (safer in extreme weather: loss rate 11.39% → 10.10%) matter less overall.
What if look-ups are limited?Exp 5 budget: with only 6 calls per query, MandiGuard earns ₹403.85 vs B4 ₹299.31 (+₹104.54).
Does it work on graded apples?Exp 3: naive B1 hits 94.14% traps; MandiGuard cuts traps to 13.24% and worst-10% from −₹8,487.24 to −₹102.76, but its mean (₹605.06) trails B2 (₹1,150.83) → explained in Stage II.
Does it work in a state it never trained on?Exp 9: beats B1 in 6 of 6 unseen states.
What if freight or rot assumptions are wrong?Exp 6: across 9 freight × spoilage combinations, beats B1 in all 9 (+₹82.62 to +₹121.42).
What if trap penalties are smaller?Exp 15: still ahead of B1 until penalties are set to exactly zero (then −₹10.00 vs B1, but loss trips 6.09% vs 18.52%).
Only on markets guaranteed open?Exp 15 matched (10,162 episodes): beats B1 (+₹38.38) and B2 (+₹40.91); B3 earns more on average (₹553.22) but with 2.2× the loss-trip rate and 10× deeper tail losses.
Does it hold over many years?Exp 10: 661,192 trips over six eras (2017–2026): loss-trip rate 8.78%–12.03% vs 39.18%–44.29% naive; +₹165.14 over B1 in the 2024 heatwave.

Chapter 10 — Stage II: The Honest Autopsy and MandiGuard-CRC

First, the most important rule Stage II was designed after seeing Stage I results, so it is labelled [POST-DIAGNOSTIC / VALIDATION-CALIBRATED]. Stage I stays frozen exactly as pre-registered. Stage II models are trained on 2024, tuned only on Jan–May 2025 validation, and then evaluated once on the untouched holdout.

10.1 Why do an autopsy?

Two things bothered us: (1) Stage I tied the simple B2 rule on average (H2 failed), and (2) it missed many profitable Grade A apple trades. Instead of hiding these, we asked “what exactly went wrong inside our own design?” (Exp 16).

10.2 Finding 1 — Hiding closed days made risky trips look safe (censored arrivals)

Analogy Judging how hard an exam was by looking only at students who turned up — the ones who stayed away (because they were unprepared) are invisible, so the exam looks easier than it was.

The Stage I model was trained only on trips where the destination recorded a price on arrival (dropna). This removed 55.83% of raw 2024 corridors. But closed days are exactly the bad outcomes! As quotes get older, the chance that the market is open on arrival drops (89.10% for fresh quotes → 62.63% for 3-day-old quotes in 2024). Ignoring the closed cases made the bad-day (20th percentile) drop look up to 2.54× smaller than it really was on holdout (−10.55% vs true −26.82%). Researchers call this the selective labels problem (Lakkaraju et al., 2017).

10.3 Finding 2 — One umbrella for all weather (coverage illusion)

Analogy Carrying the same small umbrella in a drizzle and in a storm. On average you stay “mostly dry”, but you are over-protected in drizzle and soaked in storms.

The 80% cushion was one size per crop. Overall it covered ~79%, which looked perfect. But splitting markets by how volatile they were:

Market group (holdout)CoverageCushion givenCushion needed (true 80th-pct error)
Calmest quarter (Q1)90.46%6.04%1.98%
Most volatile quarter (Q4)67.80%8.89%17.08%

So calm markets got too much cushion (good trips refused) and volatile markets too little (risky trips allowed). Validation showed the same pattern (88.91% vs 67.84%). Known in theory as heteroscedasticity (Lei et al., 2018; Romano et al., 2019).

10.4 Finding 3 — Splitting apples into thin grades fooled T1

When Himachal markets report Grade A and Grade B separately, each grade appears on fewer days, so T1’s “reported on ≥50% of days” test thought the market was inactive. Among apple lots where B2 sent a truck but MandiGuard refused, 77.82% (holdout) were blocked at T1, not by the cushion (22.18%). We had first guessed the cushion was the problem — the autopsy corrected us.

Figure 8 (thesis numbering). (A) Censored-arrival bias by quote age; (B) coverage by volatility quarter; (C) Stage II improvement ladder.

10.5 The fix: MandiGuard-CRC, built one rung at a time

Rung 0Stage I MandiGuard ₹452.79
➜
Rung 1Sort shortlist by gap minus 1.20× straight-line freight ₹455.15
➜
Rung 2Two models on full (uncensored) outcomes + risk penalty ₹469.29
➜
Rung 3 = MandiGuard-CRCGrade-aware T1 (fresh0) ₹479.17
  • Rung 1: before choosing the top 5 markets, sort them by screen gap minus an estimated freight (₹35 + ₹0.45 × 1.20 × straight-line km). Costs zero extra calls.
  • Rung 2: train two tree models on all 274,296 settled 2024 trips that passed T1 and looked profitable before costs — including closed and delayed outcomes: one predicts expected net gain (μ̂), the other predicts the probability of losing money (p̂loss).
  • Rung 3: “fresh0” rule — a same-day exact quote (age 0) can pass T1 with relaxed history (≥20% of last 14 days, ≥25% same-weekday), alongside the normal strict rule. This rescues thinly reported grades.
The CRC score Score = μ̂ − λ × (local price) × p̂_loss DISPATCH only if Score > ₹50 and μ̂ > ₹50 Example A (safe route): μ̂ = +₹320, p̂loss = 0.08, local ₹1,400 → penalty 0.15 × 1,400 × 0.08 = ₹16.80 → Score +₹303.20 → DISPATCH.
Example B (stale volatile route): μ̂ = +₹140, p̂loss = 0.55 → penalty 0.15 × 1,400 × 0.55 = ₹115.50 → Score +₹24.50 < ₹50 → REFUSE. (These two are teaching illustrations of the formula.)

10.6 How λ (the risk weight) was chosen — validation only

  1. Try λ = 0.00, 0.05, 0.10, …, 1.20 (25 values) on the Jan–May 2025 validation set (42,794 episodes).
  2. For each λ, count dispatched trucks and loss trips. Compute (losses + 1) / (dispatches + 1).
  3. Stop at the first λ where this ratio is ≤ 0.095 (9.5%). Result: λ* = 0.15 for MandiGuard-CRC (validation loss ratio 9.15%, mean ₹365.46); λ* = 0.10 for Rung 2.
  4. Freeze λ and evaluate once on the holdout.

This calibration idea comes from Conformal Risk Control (Angelopoulos et al., 2024). We use it as a practical validation recipe and do not claim its mathematical guarantee, because crop prices change across seasons (not “exchangeable”) and the number of dispatches changes with λ.

10.7 Stage II results on data it never saw

Test setMandiGuard-CRCComparison
Holdout, 69,526 episodes₹479.17/qtl (₹14,375 per truck), loss trips 10.48%+₹129.16 vs B1 (p=0.0004); +₹32.51 vs B2 (95% CI +12.05 to +50.49, p=0.0016); +₹26.38 vs Stage I (p=0.0002)
Guaranteed-open markets, 10,162 episodes (no modelled penalties)₹533.75, loss trips 7.14%+₹22.86 vs Stage I, +₹61.24 vs B1, +₹63.76 vs B2; B3 still higher mean (₹553.22) at 14.77% loss trips
HP graded apples, 1,537 lots₹812.08 (+34.2% vs Stage I)Grade A: ₹205.46 → ₹477.56, loss trips 20.0% → 11.54%; still below B2 (₹1,150.83) but worst-10% −₹113.40 vs −₹272.50
Why Stage II is not overfitting (say this) “The models were trained on 2024 only, the single setting λ was chosen on validation only, and the holdout was used once. We also checked the guaranteed-open subset with zero modelled penalties, so the gain is not just an artefact of how we scored closed markets. And Stage I remains the pre-registered headline.”

The research gap in one line Economics shows information alone does not help without reliable selling; computer science forecasts prices but treats closed days as noise and uses straight-line distance; machine-learning theory offers abstention and cushions but had not been applied to this decision. This thesis joins the three and measures the result on real Indian data.

Chapter 12 — What We Did Differently, and Limitations

12.1 Typical approach vs this thesis

AspectTypical mandi app / prior studyThis thesis
GoalPredict tomorrow’s priceDecide: send the truck or stay home
Closed marketsRemoved as noise or filled inChecked first (T1) and studied as the main risk
Variety / gradeOften mergedExact variety; grade-aware rule in Stage II
DistanceStraight lineReal roads (OSRM), hill multiplier
SpoilageIgnored, or weather used only for priceHeat/rain spoilage on the actual route
UncertaintySingle number80% cushion from recent real errors; risk penalty in Stage II
Option to refuseNoYes — explicit “stay home”
EvaluationForecast error (MSE)Money, loss-trip rate, worst-10%, calls; on unseen months
HonestyResults after the factPre-registered H1–H4; failed H2 reported; Stage II clearly labelled

12.2 The precise contributions (what is new)

  1. Measurement: a multi-state, multi-crop measurement (6 states, 4 crops, 2017–2026) of how much screen spread is phantom, with official parity checks.
  2. Government-grounded profit model and a two-view check of how much results depend on modelled penalties.
  3. Stage I MandiGuard: a pre-registered, transparent cheap-first verification cascade with a causal 80% cushion and a refuse option (H1, H3, H4 supported).
  4. Stage II autopsy: three measured failure mechanisms (censored arrivals, coverage illusion, thin-grade T1).
  5. Stage II MandiGuard-CRC: uncensored two-model scoring with a validation-calibrated risk weight and grade-aware T1, beating B2 on unseen data.
What is NOT new (say it before the examiner does) We did not invent conformal prediction, Conformal Risk Control, gradient boosting, OSRM or the Q10 rule. We did not prove a new theorem. The novelty is in applying and combining these to a real decision problem, measuring it carefully on Indian data, and diagnosing why it works or fails.

12.3 Limitations (say them calmly and confidently)

LimitationWhat it means / how we addressed it
1. Field costs are modelledTruck rates (₹35 + ₹0.45/km), Q10 spoilage and closed-market penalties are not from real receipts. Sensitivity tests (Exp 6, Exp 15) show how results change.
2. Tests check code, not the real world22/22 tests prove correctness and reproducibility, not real farm economics.
3. Mirror data, sample checksBulk data came from an archive mirror; verified on 172 + 2,042 official keys, not every row of every year.
4. Unobserved local factorsTrader credit ties, queues, tolls and same-day gluts are not in daily tables. On guaranteed-open markets, point-ML still has a higher average (with much higher risk).
5. Stage II is post-diagnosticDesigned after Stage I results; no theoretical guarantee claimed because prices are not exchangeable.
6. Apples still conservativeMandiGuard-CRC sends fewer apple trucks than B2 (22.84% vs 33.64%) and earns less on average there.

Future work: field pilots with farmer producer organisations (FPOs) and real weighment receipts; adaptive cushions per volatility level; SMS delivery for feature phones (illustrated in the appendix experiments); extension to more states and crops.

13.1 One-minute pitch (memorise)

“Price portals show farmers that distant mandis pay more, but across 63,040 naive dispatches a ₹1,330 screen gap shrank to ₹386, and 40% of trucks lost money, mostly because markets were closed or not buying the exact variety. I built MandiGuard, a transparent checklist that verifies market activity first, then roads, weather, and a frozen model with an 80% safety cushion, and refuses risky trips. On 69,526 unseen opportunities, with hypotheses pre-registered, it earned ₹102.78 per quintal more than naive chasing, cut loss episodes by 37 points versus point-ML, and used 44% fewer look-ups. It only tied a strong fresh-road rule on average, so I diagnosed three causes and built MandiGuard-CRC, which, tuned only on validation, reached ₹479.17 per quintal and beat that rule by ₹32.51. Costs like freight and spoilage are still modelled, so field pilots are the next step.”

13.2 Presentation tips

  • Start with the farmer, not the algorithm. Examiners remember stories.
  • Always say the unit: “rupees per quintal”, and translate to a 30-quintal truck when it helps.
  • When showing H2, say “not supported” clearly — honesty builds trust.
  • Keep Stage I and Stage II visually separate (two colours on slides).
  • Have the T1–T4 flowchart and the Tomato arithmetic ready to draw on a whiteboard.

Chapter 14 — Viva Defence: 35 Likely Questions

Answer in this pattern: direct answer → one number → one honest boundary. Keep it short; offer detail only if asked.

Q1. What is “Phantom Spatial Arbitrage”?
The part of a price gap between two mandis that looks profitable on screen but disappears after closed markets, missing varieties, freight, fees, spoilage and arrival-day price drops are counted.
Q2. Why did you choose this topic?
High stakes for small farmers, a clear gap between economics and forecasting research, fully public data, and a method small enough to build and defend in an M.Tech.
Q3. Why not just build a better price predictor?
Because the biggest loss (₹714.90/qtl in Exp 1) comes from execution traps, not forecast error. On guaranteed-open markets point-ML predicts well, but on real markets it lost money on 45.28% of trips.
Q4. Is refusing really a good outcome?
Yes. Chow (1970) showed abstaining is optimal when errors are costly. Staying home costs ₹0 extra; a bad trip loses diesel, produce and time.
Q5. Is your data real?
Yes: AGMARKNET prices, OSRM roads, ERA5/NASA weather and government reports. No synthetic prices. Costs like truck hire are modelled and clearly labelled.
Q6. How do you know the mirror data matches the government?
Exp 14: 172 keys from data.gov.in XML (Min/Max 100%, Modal 99.42%) and 2,042 keys over 149 days from AGMARKNET 2.0 (all three 100%).
Q7. How did you prevent data leakage?
Time splits (train 2024, validate Jan–May 2025, test after), model frozen after 2024, cushion updated only from trips already arrived, markets selected using 2024 only, and an automatic leakage assertion in code.
Q8. Why an 80% cushion and a ₹50 margin?
80% is a standard, interpretable coverage level and was verified empirically (78.85% val, 79.07% holdout). ₹50 was chosen from {50,...,250} on validation only.
Q9. What is conformal prediction in one line?
Use the model’s recent real errors to build a cushion so that roughly the chosen fraction (80%) of future outcomes lie above the cautious estimate.
Q10. Why a gradient-boosted tree model?
Fast, strong on tabular data, handles non-linear patterns, and is easy to freeze and audit. Alternatives were tried in the appendix (Exp 11).
Q11. Why did H2 fail?
MandiGuard sends fewer trucks than B2, trading average profit for safety: loss trips 9.97% vs 18.11%, worst-10% −₹37.89 vs −₹436.67. The +₹6.13 average difference is within noise.
Q12. Isn’t H4 (fewer calls) obvious?
Partly yes, by design. The real benefit shows under tight budgets: with 6 calls, MandiGuard beats B4 by ₹104.54/qtl.
Q13. Are the closed-market penalties made up?
They are modelled rules. Exp 15 reduces them to half and to zero, and tests guaranteed-open markets with no penalties; conclusions vs B1 hold until penalties are exactly zero.
Q14. Why does point-ML win on open markets?
When every market is open, price prediction is the main skill and B3 dispatches more. But it does so with 2.2× the loss-trip rate and 10× deeper tail losses.
Q15. What is CVaR / worst-10%?
The average of the worst 10% of outcomes — how bad the bad days are.
Q16. Why a two-way cluster bootstrap?
Outcomes in the same market and same fortnight are related; resampling whole mandis and whole 2-week blocks gives honest uncertainty.
Q17. Why Holm correction?
Testing four hypotheses increases the chance of a lucky win; Holm keeps the overall false-positive rate at 5%.
Q18. What is pre-registration?
Writing hypotheses before seeing test data (commit e421d15) so the story cannot be changed afterwards.
Q19. What did Stage II discover?
Three causes: dropping closed arrivals hid bad outcomes (up to 2.54× understated risk), one cushion size over-protected calm and under-protected volatile markets (90.46% vs 67.80%), and thin apple grades fooled T1 (77.82% of missed apple trades).
Q20. What is the selective labels problem?
When you only see outcomes for some cases (here: days the market reported), and those cases are not random, your model learns a too-optimistic picture (Lakkaraju et al., 2017).
Q21. What does the CRC score do?
Score = expected gain − λ × local price × probability of loss. It penalises routes that might lose money in proportion to what is at stake.
Q22. How was λ = 0.15 chosen?
On validation only: try 0 to 1.20 in steps of 0.05 and take the first value where (losses+1)/(dispatches+1) ≤ 9.5%.
Q23. Do you claim the CRC theorem guarantee?
No. Crop prices are not exchangeable across seasons and the number of dispatches changes with λ, so we use CRC as a validation recipe and check it on holdout.
Q24. Isn’t Stage II overfitting to the holdout?
No holdout tuning: trained on 2024, λ chosen on validation, holdout used once; also checked on guaranteed-open markets with no modelled penalties.
Q25. Why keep Stage I if Stage II is better?
Stage I is the pre-registered confirmatory result. Replacing it would be HARKing. Stage II is reported separately as a post-diagnostic improvement.
Q26. Why does MandiGuard-CRC still trail B2 on apples?
It sends fewer apple trucks (22.84% vs 33.64%). B2 earns more on average but with 28.43% loss trips and a much deeper worst-10% (−₹272.50 vs −₹113.40).
Q27. Is MandiGuard an AI agent or uses ChatGPT?
No. No LLM and no reinforcement learning. It is a deterministic checklist plus one frozen tree model and a cushion.
Q28. What do your 22 tests prove?
That the code is deterministic, splits are leak-free, files match checksums, and results are consistent — not that real-world costs are correct.
Q29. What is your biggest limitation?
Freight, spoilage and closed-market penalties are modelled from government averages, not measured from real farmer receipts.
Q30. Does it work in new states?
Exp 9: trained on 5 states and tested on the 6th, it beat naive chasing in all 6 cases.
Q31. Does it work across years and shocks?
Exp 10: 661,192 trips over 2017–2026 (GST, COVID, export curbs, 2024 heatwave), loss-trip rate stayed 8.78%–12.03%.
Q32. What exactly is novel?
Measuring the phantom across states and crops with official checks; a pre-registered verify-first cascade with a refuse option; a measured autopsy of its failures; and a validation-calibrated uncensored fix. The tools are known; the problem framing, combination and evidence are new.
Q33. How would a farmer use it?
As a morning advisory (app or SMS) saying “send to market X” or “sell locally today”, ideally through an FPO; the appendix illustrates SMS cards and FPO truck sharing.
Q34. What would you do next?
Field pilot with real receipts, volatility-aware cushions, more states and crops, and an SMS/FPO deployment study.
Q35. If you had to drop one gate, which?
T2 or T3 have the smallest overall effect (+₹0.44 for T2), though T3 helps in extreme weather. T1 and T4 should never be dropped.

14.1 Five red lines — never say these

Avoid these over-claims
  1. “Conformal/CRC gives a guaranteed bound in our setting.” → It does not; prices are not exchangeable. Say “empirically calibrated and checked on holdout.”
  2. “MandiGuard-CRC was pre-registered.” → Only Stage I was. Stage II is post-diagnostic.
  3. “It is an autonomous AI agent” or “it beats point-ML on open markets on average.” → Neither is true.
  4. “Our costs are verified with farmers.” → They are modelled; tests check code, not field economics.
  5. “The appendix experiments (ACI, ZeroCloud, FPO) are main contributions.” → They are illustrations only.

Coverage% of real outcomes that land above the cautious estimate

BootstrapRe-drawing data many times to measure uncertainty
Holm correctionStricter significance when testing several hypotheses

CRC, λConformal Risk Control; the risk weight tuned on validation
fresh0Stage II rule letting same-day quotes pass T1 with relaxed history

The final message Information is free, but information is not money. Verified, cautious decisions — including the courage to say “stay home” — are what protect a small farmer. This thesis measured the problem honestly, built a transparent solution, tested it fairly, admitted where it fell short, and fixed what it could, while clearly stating what still needs real-world proof.
